title: DHCP Relay: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: You have one D H C P server. And many subnets. But broadcasts never cross a router. So how does a new device ever get an address?

scenes.heading: The campus mailroom
scenes.narration: A university has one central post office and lots of buildings. A student in the science building drops a request in the local mailroom. The clerk can't shout across campus, so they write a proper addressed envelope to the central post office. They also stamp it with the science building's return address, so the post office knows which pool of addresses to use. That clerk is the relay agent, and the return address is called the giaddr.

scenes.heading: The command
scenes.narration: The magic command is I P helper address. It goes on the interface facing the clients, not the one facing the server. And you can add more than one, for backup.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. The relay doesn't pass the broadcast along. It creates a brand new unicast to the server. The giaddr holds the relay's own address, not the client's, because the client has none yet. And helper address goes on the client facing interface.

items.wrong: Relay forwards the broadcast as a broadcast
items.right: It sends a new unicast to the server
It's the relay's address on the client's subnet

items.wrong: Helper goes on the server-facing side
items.right: It goes on the client-facing interface

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva DHCP relay lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A relay lets one D H C P server serve many subnets. The helper address goes on the client facing interface. And the giaddr tells the server which pool to use. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva DHCP relay lab.
